newsitem.title: FRANCE: Stocks tumble, Juppe wavers on shock French vote.
newsitem.headline: Stocks tumble, Juppe wavers on shock French vote.

text.p: French stocks plunged on Monday and Prime Minister Alain Juppe hinted President Jacques Chirac may have to replace him after the left-wing opposition outpolled his centre-right coalition in a parliamentary election first round.

The Paris Bourse opened 3.84 percent down and the CAC-40 blue chip share index settled more than three percent off as anxious traders weighed the risk of an upset left-wing victory in next Sunday's decisive runoff, a prospect financial markets had largely ignored.

But there was no panic on currency markets, which expect a Socialist-led government would go ahead with a single European currency if elected. The franc slipped to 3.3773 per mark in early trading but recovered to 3.3745, less than a centime lower than last Friday's close.

The morning after his RPR-UDF alliance suffered a stinging rebuff from voters, Juppe said he was convinced Chirac would make the right choice if a change of personality were needed for the centre-right coalition to win the election.

"If the sole obstacle to the modernisation and renovation of France is a choice of personality, I am quite convinced the president will know how to make the right choice," he told reporters in Bordeaux, where a Socialist challenger forced him into a runoff in his adopted constituency.
Responding to veiled calls for his removal, the prime minister said: "What is at stake is not Alain Juppe but France."
Chirac aides said the president was consulting political leaders by telephone and analysing the first-round results in a "calm, studious and thoughtful" atmosphere.
Coalition leaders said they expected the president to make a solemn appeal to voters later in the week.
Whatever the outcome of next Sunday's second round, Juppe said his government would tender its resignation to Chirac, in line with French tradition.

Official Interior Ministry results showed the combined left polled 40.22 percent of the vote, the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition and other moderate rightists 36.50 percent and the extreme-right National Front 14.94 percent. Ecologists scored 6.81 percent.
The left's score is more than 44 percent if the Greens, the biggest ecologist group which has an electoral pact with the Socialists, are added.

Left-wing parties across Europe rejoiced at their French comrades' gains. German Social Democratic opposition leader Oskar Lafontaine said it showed that "economic and financial policies which raise unemployment through restrictive budgets and social spending cuts are condemned to failure".

Polling institutes projected the left would win a wafer-thin overall majority if Sunday's pattern were repeated in the runoff, but they stressed the election was wide open with the difference in seats between the two blocs equivalent to less than one percentage point of the popular vote.

Much will depend on how National Front supporters vote in the 444 constituencies where their candidate failed to qualify for the runoff, and on whether the right can mobilise some of the 32.09 percent of voters who abstained.
National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who called on Chirac to resign after Sunday's massive protest vote, was due to announce his position on the second round later on Monday.
Juppe's fellow Gaullist rival, outgoing National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, hinted it might be time to change premiers given Sunday's election warning.
As the right licked its wounds, Seguin, France's best-known Eurosceptic, forecast that the coalition would end up at best with a five or six-seat majority.

"You don't change campaign leaders in mid-watch, but given that one of the best hypotheses is that the centre-right could win a majority of a few seats, the problems at stake are different from those posed by a hundred-seat advance," he said.
Gaullist ex-budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy said that to blame Juppe alone would be missing the point.
"Looking for a scapegoat would not allow us to find the true answers to the citizens' discontent. The ruling coalition as a whole has been taught a lesson," he told France-Inter radio.

The left pledged vigorous state job-creation measures and a shorter working week without loss of pay to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment. The coalition promised market reforms to scale down state control, cut taxes and free private enterprise.

Ministers dubbed the vote a "warning", a "rebuke" or a "slap on the wrist" after two years of austerity, high taxes and unemployment but insisted it did not mean voters really wanted a return to the Socialist-Communist government of the early 1980s.

There was no triumphalism on the left. Socialist leader Lionel Jospin ordered his troops to stay cautious and modest, and Socialist politicians stressed they still had to convince the electorate they were capable of bring about real change.
The vote put pressure on Chirac to intervene again in the election, in which he gambled his presidency 10 months before his giant parliamentary majority needed to face voters.

"Naming a new prime minister would appear like capitulation to the enemy," said political commentator Alain Duhamel. "Chirac could however give two or three personalities a more prominent role, like (former premier) Edouard Balladur or Seguin."
